newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ricky's tattoos make HK handover indelible moment. [CORRECTED 10:54 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Ricky's tattoos make HK handover indelible moment. [CORRECTED 10:54 GMT]

text.p: Two bleary-eyed British sailors nicknamed Cockles and Seb stumbled down the stairs of Ricky's Tattoo Parlour in Hong Kong and out onto the neon-lit streets of the Wan Chai nightlife district.
They were feeling no pain from an evening out on the town -- except for the Chinese characters both had just had tattooed across the tops of their right feet.
"Hurts like a bastard I can tell you," said 20-year old Cockles, removing a shoe, sock and temporary gauze bandage to show off the latest addition to his growing collection of body art.

There on the foot against a backdrop of angry red skin were delicate Chinese characters inscribed in black ink. "Mine says 'Cockles and Seb' and my mate's says 'Seb and Cockles'," the sailor said. "At least that's what they're supposed to say. We can't read Chinese, can you?"
The pair of sailors are most proud of the 'Hong Kong 1997' they recently had tattooed on their upper biceps to commemorate Britain's transfer of the territory back to China at midnight on June 30.
Their ship, HMS Chatham, will be the last British military vessel to depart Hong Kong after a colonial interlude of more than 150 years.
Tens of thousands of servicemen, tourists and Triad (gang) members have had tattoos in Hong Kong over the years.
Arguably, no tattoo parlour in the world is more famous than Ricky's. The sign over his tatty stairwell reads "Expert in Improving Misfit Tattoos. Tops In Colours, Skill and Designs."
"Our reputation spread all over the world by word of mouth," said 60-year old Ricky, who runs the parlour with his elder brother Pinky.
"The wars in Korea and Vietnam brought navies into Hong Kong and the sailors went home and told their friends. Our designs are interesting and our technique is good so we get a lot of business."
The walls of the brightly-lit parlour are covered with sample designs and a coffee table is piled high with books containing more.
Among the Union Jacks, snakes, lizards, flowers, naked women and fish there's even an archetypal anchor with 'U.S. Navy' underneath.
There are also scores of photographs of men and women who have opted for tattoos far more colourful and elaborate than the ones chosen by Cockles and Seb.

Some photographs show entire bodies covered -- chest, back, legs and upper arms -- with intricate dragons, vines and blossoms. Ambitious designs can take 12 hours to execute and cost thousands of dollars.
And while getting a tattoo has been part of the male bonding process among servicemen for generations, women also partake.
Louise Howard, a 41-year-old tourist from Essex in east England, recently opted for a dragon with 'Hong Kong 1997' emblazoned underneath.
Ricky did the dragon and an assistant did the lettering. The entire process took about 40-minutes and cost US $150.

Howard (Corrects from Wright) seemed mildly uncomfortable while Ricky was dipping the point of his electric needle gun into small pots of coloured ink and poking it into her skin to transfer the design, but she beamed with delight at the finished product.
"My father was a sailor in the British navy and he chickened out on getting a tattoo so I thought I'd get one for him," she said.

"I just thought that since I'm in Hong Kong and Ricky's is famous I should get one done here and now...I chose the Chinese dragon and 'Hong Kong 1997' because it is a date to remember, a bit of international history and I'm a part of it."
Asked what her husband thought of her getting a tattoo Wright replied: "Well, it's my second tattoo and both my husband and my mother are of the same opinion. They think tattoos are barbaric."

Ricky's is clean and bright but would hardly be mistaken for a smart beauty salon on the upper East Side in New York or in London's Knightsbridge district. Then again, that might spoil the experience.
